title: Driving the Wrong Way: Leveraging Interpretability in End2End Autonomous Driving Models
models: GTRS (trajectory-scoring end-to-end driving model with per-subscore heads, builds on Hydra-MDP with diffusion trajectory generation)
action_head: n/a (trajectory vocabulary scoring / generation, not a VLA)
methods: SAEs (TopK, Matryoshka, Archetypal) inserted into the latent space, compared on reconstruction, dead neurons, ego-status correlation/probing and downstream EPDMS
neuron maximization and neuron clustering for concept labeling
concept-conditioned relevance propagation (CRP) to camera inputs
circuit analysis from SAE neurons to scoring heads
question: Can SAE concepts inside end-to-end driving models explain how candidate trajectories are scored, reveal spurious logic, and be edited to improve driving metrics?
key_findings: TopK SAEs beat Matryoshka and Archetypal SAEs on ego-status disentanglement; archetypal SAEs appear to memorize correlated NAVSIM scenes; mid-sized dictionaries reconstruct best (Table I, qualitative summary).

SAE neuron clusters correspond to concepts such as intersections/lane markings, following a lead vehicle, straight roads; activation and attribution rankings differ, so highly active concepts are not necessarily used for the chosen trajectory.

Circuit analysis shows 'car ahead' neurons influence all GTRS scoring heads, including traffic-light compliance, which the authors read as a spurious correlation (lead vehicles co-occur with intersections).
Removing iPad's backward-facing camera does not change SAE activations and there is no measurable gradient to it, suggesting the camera is unused.

Zero-ablating three SAE neurons {177, 59, 71} raises EPDMS from 0.4963 (with SAE) to 0.5926, above the original model without SAE (0.524); drivable-area compliance +0.130, at-fault collisions +0.054, but ego progress -0.100 (Table II).

evidence.setting: offline dataset only (NAVSIM non-reactive evaluation of predicted trajectories)
evidence.scale: NAVSIM evaluation split (size not stated in the parts read); single ablation configuration
evidence.baselines: model with unmodified SAE; original model without SAE

causal_validation: Yes: zero-ablation of selected SAE neurons changes predicted trajectories and improves scored driving metrics; circuit attributions to heads are gradient-based.
closed_loop: No in the strict sense: NAVSIM scores planned trajectories against logged scenes without a reactive closed loop, although the paper speaks of 'improved closed-loop behavior'.
limitations_stated: Relevance maps can be misleading (distributed features, non-local concepts like weather, convolutional stride artifacts).
Penalty heads predict absence of violations, which makes activation-based interpretation harder.
critique: Shows the full SAE pipeline (selection, labeling, circuit to heads, targeted ablation) giving a measurable metric gain, which few VLA SAE papers achieve.
The ablated neurons appear to be chosen with knowledge of downstream scores and evaluated on NAVSIM; it is not stated that selection and evaluation use disjoint data, so the gain may be optimistic.
The gain partly trades progress for conservatism (ego progress -0.10), so 'removing erroneous behavior' may be a shift along a safety-progress trade-off rather than a fix.
Driving models with trajectory scoring heads, not VLAs; the per-subscore head design is highlighted as an interpretability advantage worth noting for VLA architecture design.
one_line: Inserting a TopK SAE into the GTRS driving model exposes concepts like 'car ahead' and spurious links such as car-ahead to traffic-light compliance, and zero-ablating three SAE neurons raises the NAVSIM EPDMS from 0.50 to 0.59 at some cost in progress.
